name: pc-screen-control
description: A screenshot is a picture made for human eyes. This hands you the screen as data instead - so you press the right button by name, know it worked, and hardly ever need the user's mouse to do it.
long_description: Use this INSTEAD of taking a screenshot and clicking a coordinate. Windows already publishes what is on screen as structured data - every button, field and list with its name and state, the same thing screen readers read - and this hands it to you directly. That means three things. You press the right thing, because controls are found by name and not by pixel, so nothing drifts when a window moves. You know whether it worked, because every action returns the element's state before and after. And the user keeps their mouse, because reading the tree and operating controls go through the accessibility interface rather than the pointer - they can carry on working while you work. Start every desktop task with describe_screen. 34 tools: read the tree, operate controls, read tables as rows and columns, set sliders to an exact number, move and resize windows, read and write the clipboard, open menus. A window you have claimed is different again: it sits past the edge of every monitor, so it cannot be seen and the user's pointer cannot reach it - and therefore invoke, set_text, toggle, expand, select and set_value on a claimed window take NO block at all, no pulse, no held input. Park a window once and work in it without interrupting anybody; that is the cheapest mode this server has and it is worth reaching for before anything that needs the foreground. Coordinate input and screen capture remain as a documented fallback for surfaces that genuinely paint themselves, such as editing canvases and games. Prefer the pattern route always: no tool steps down to the keyboard or the pointer without saying so, and invoke refuses rather than clicking behind your back, so reach for click, drag or send_keys only when a tool has told you there is no cheaper way. Taking the screen is a BLOCK, not a per-action grab, and this is on you to use: call set_guard block:'start' (with estimate_seconds when you already know it will take a while) before a run of actions that need the screen or the foreground, and block:'end' the instant you no longer need control - while you think, read, or work in the background. Everything between is ONE takeover instead of one interruption per action, which is the difference between the user being disturbed once and being disturbed ten times; forgetting is safe but scatters the work back into flicker. While a block is held the user sees a red pulse at the screen edge, deepening then fading to blue, plus a Windows notification saying what you are doing and how long - a message in the chat is not a warning, because they are working in another window. Their input is held and their window, focus, text cursor and mouse position are restored when the block ends. focus_window obeys the same rule, so nothing takes the foreground silently. set_guard priority:'me' makes you wait for their go and refuse rather than take over; set_guard await_user:'...' hands the screen back and asks them, on screen, to do what only they can - a login, a password - while you wait or work elsewhere. The user can pause, stop, or switch to watching from a tray icon at any time, including while a block is held - the taskbar is deliberately left out of the input hold, so their way out is never blocked by yours. Work out the whole sequence BEFORE you open a block - the refs, the text, the order - then run it with batch in one call rather than one tool at a time: between two calls you are thinking, and while you think the screen is still occupied, so a job of five predictable steps can cost the user a minute of waiting for ten seconds of work. Reading is free and opens no block, so look first and act second; taking control and then starting to look around is what turns a ten-second job into a two-minute freeze. Never leave a long wait inside a block - end it, wait while they work, open a new one when the screen is ready; batch now REFUSES a wait longer than 2 seconds for exactly this reason, so split the batch rather than making somebody sit through it. If something unexpected turns up, hand the screen back BEFORE working out what to do, not after. Long text belongs in the clipboard before the block starts, not typed key by key inside it. And never send keystrokes blind on force: check that the field you mean actually has focus, or pass a ref - a message typed into the wrong window is the one mistake this whole design exists to prevent. The server now enforces that for you: the window you last acted in is remembered, and blind keystrokes or clicks are REFUSED if something else is in front - which is what happens when a block ended while you were thinking and the screen went back to the user. If you see that refusal, do not force it: call focus_window on your window again, or pass a ref. It means the person is somewhere else and your keystrokes were about to land in their work. The window they were in when the block started is protected the same way and by the server, not by you: closing it, parking it out of reach and minimising it are all REFUSED, an ambiguous window_title is refused rather than guessed for anything destructive, and Alt+F4 or Ctrl+W without a ref is refused because blind it closes whatever holds the keyboard. If their window does not come back to the front when a block ends, the next call you make says so and names it - fix that with focus_window before doing anything else, because they are looking at a window you raised. set_guard block:'end' answers this directly: it reports handed_back with whether the foreground came back, which window is in front now, and whether the caret was restored - all measured after the fact, so 'they have their screen back' is something you can read rather than assume. block:'start' answers the other half: input_held says whether the user's keyboard and mouse are REALLY held. If it is false, Windows refused the input hooks and you are on a shared screen - never type without a ref, keep the block short, and say so. This server makes NO network connection of any kind - no update check, no telemetry, nothing; checking for a newer version is a separate program the user runs by hand. launch_app is not a general shell: it refuses shell commands and URLs unless confirm:true. Password fields are read back as a placeholder, never their contents. Windows only.
